Can someone please ELI5 why this seems so difficult for them?

  • the game uses Unreal Engine 3, which supports consoles and PC;
  • unlike the previous console generation, XB1 and PS4 are both x86 machines (PS4 has all off-the-shelf parts); and
  • they have done this twice before already - the PC port for Arkham City was great.

I read the full article, it doesn't give any insight. I googled, top hits just talk about PC ports getting nerfed because piracy blah blah. I would like to believe that Rocksteady/WB are serious about getting this done. Obviously I'm missing something. What makes it so difficult?

Consoles basically only have a few hardware options. They're also usually framerate locked to something terrible like 30. (newer ones can do 60, but that doesn't mean they wrote the game to do it.) They also have pretty much 0 configuration for video and control settings. So, devs can take all kinds of shortcuts and get away with crap that'll only work on console hardware.

Then they actually run it on one of the infinite permutations of PC hardware that's been out for the last 5 years and things fall apart. Framerate issues, control configuration issues, video configuration issues, there's a myriad of things that can go wrong.

Thanks mate. I think that's a great, succinct explanation for why PC releases often lag behind. I hadn't stopped to appreciate massive additional workload that multiple configurations create for testers, so cheers for that.

Glad I could help!

It takes a lot of planning and a lot of discipline. There's a reason PC titles frequently get pushed back by more reliable companies like Valve. Sometimes, even with all of that planning, you still run into issues that soak up a lot of time. As I said, there are a lot of things to test, and that means a lot of time spent on testing, fixing bugs found by testing, and re-testing fixed bugs. This is all in addition to investing in properly designing things in the first place.

Unfortunately, what can sometimes happen at big publishers is that they behave similar to movie studios. "Wow, that game made a lot of money. We need a sequel and we need it in five years." Then they pick a release date before they've even finished filming. Big publishers have started doing this kind of thing. They want another game released ASAP, so they set some arbitrary release date and then tell the dev team they have to hit it. Sadly this frequently forces the dev team to skip a lot of steps, and you end up with an extremely low-quality release. It's not like the devs don't know, or that they're happy about it, they just aren't given a choice.

So, yeah, I would never pre-order anything. I always wait until all of the bugs have been worked out, which also usually coincides with the first time the game really goes on sale on Steam. There have been games I was really excited about that I waited to purchase and I was extremely glad that I did, because they were nearly unplayable at launch and then never improved much after that. Sadly things won't change until people stop pre-ordering and stop buying half-baked games.

The digital age of photography has turned me off to post processing. My limited formal education in art and photography started well after the digital revolution. My instructor insisted we learn the basics using a single black and white roll of film per assignment. Each assignment had a theme and 2-3 different criteria. These criteria ranged from specific subjects to compositions, etc. All photographs were developed and processed by hand in our tiny lab. You had to present a selected number of your photographs (6? IIRC) to the class and justify how the met the assignment criteria.

Yeah, I know I sound like a crusty old shit who had to walk uphill both ways to go to school. Yadda, yadda, yadda. The adjustments I made during development were post processing and I'm a hypocrite. But, I don't see a lot of the post processing in today's media as positive. Insert Blank Here Porn has become an internet staple. But, I see many of these images as overly edited parodies of a scene/subject.

I've noticed is that a good portion of these images are overly stylized or over saturated, and lose a lot of beauty/meaning for me. This rings especially true when presented by amateurs or the inexperienced. The post processing comes off to me as overwhelming the subject rather than enhancing it. I think post processing shouldn't be noticed by the viewer unless its done in an intriguing or original way that gives the viewer something else to ponder.

I would love to learn more about post processing to grow myself. I could very well be talking out of my ass.
How do YOU effectively post process?

You're not alone in feeling that post processing can sometimes overwhelm the subject and flat out ruin an image. Often times many "newbies" go too far in every direction trying to make an image look like more than what it actually is.

On the contrary however, post processing in and of itself is an art form just as much as photography is. For example, two photographers could take the EXACT same photograph, process it with his or her unique style and yield a result that conveys two entirely different moods.

Personally I think that one of the hardest parts of processing is finding out your own "style". You want to try everything but you want it to look good. Eventually though you'll find what works for you, what you like, and what your clients like.

As this subreddit gets more active, you'll get a better insight into what users like and dislike. Popular styles. Certain techniques and other helpful information that will help you define your style in todays day and age of digital photography.

I am the same. I am a real estate photographer, so I have to use a lot of HDRI, because I can't really lug lighting equipment around everywhere I go. The problem is that I despise most HDR photography, because it looks over processed. All I want at the end of the day is to have photos where you can see the inside of the house and out the windows.
